bib.title: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists, Chapter 5: Classification
bib.venue: O'Reilly book chapter (copyright line: Datastats, LLC)

question: How do data scientists classify records into 0/1 (or few) classes, estimate propensities, evaluate classifiers, and handle rare classes?
contributions: Explains naive Bayes, linear discriminant analysis, logistic regression/GLMs, classification metrics (confusion matrix, precision, recall, specificity, ROC, AUC, lift) and imbalanced-data strategies, with R examples on loan data.

results.claim: Logistic model fitted to a balanced training set predicts roughly half as defaults; the same model type trained on the full (95% paid-off) data predicts almost none.
results.setup: Lending-club style personal loan data (R, glm/lda/klaR); balanced training set unless stated; full_model glm on unbalanced train_set, share with predicted log-odds > 0
results.quote: Only 0.39% of the loans are predicted to be in default, or less than 1/12 of the expected number.

results.claim: Weighting defaulted loans by 1/p restores predicted default share.
results.setup: glm with weight=wt (default weight 1/mean(default), others 1) on full loan_all_data
results.quote: The mean of the predicted values is now 43% instead of 0.39%.

results.claim: Default rate in the full loan data is about 5%.
results.quote: In the full data set, only about 5% of the loans were in default:

results.claim: The example logistic GAM/linear model has weak ranking ability.
results.setup: Loan data, ROC computed on training predictions
results.quote: The model has an AUC of about 0.59, corresponding to a relatively weak classifier.

results.claim: At specificity of at least 50%, recall is about 75% on the ROC curve read.
results.quote: if we want a classifier with a specificity of at least 50%, then the recall is about 75%.

results.claim: Coefficient for purpose_small_business is 1.21226 on the log-odds scale (about 3.4x odds vs credit_card).
results.setup: logistic regression, outcome ~ payment_inc_ratio + purpose_ + home_ + emp_len_ + borrower_score, family binomial, 46272 obs
results.quote:
the regression coefficient for
purpose_small_business is 1.21226.
results.note: The text says the coefficient 'reduces' the odds of defaulting; the sign is positive so it increases them. The exponentiated factor is missing from the extracted text, so exp(1.21226)=3.36 is not from the source.
results.where: Interpreting the Coefficients and Odds Ratios

results.quote:
the default risk from the borrowers with the poorest
creditworthiness is 100 times greater than that of the best borrowers!
results.note: Chapter text prints coefficient -4.63890 (and -4.638902 in summary); exp(4.64) is ~103.

results.quote: Residual deviance: 58531  on 46260  degrees of freedom
results.note: Short print gives 58530 and AIC 58550; summary gives 58531 and AIC 58555.

results.claim: Confusion matrix of logistic_gam applied to the training set.
results.setup: Loan data; rows true, columns predicted
results.note: Prose says '6,126 defaulted loans were correctly predicted ... 17,010 incorrectly predicted as paid off', which does not match the printed matrix (14635 TP, 8501 FN).

results.claim: Full-data naive Bayes posterior for a small-business, mortgage, >1 year loan is 0.628 default.
results.setup: klaR NaiveBayes on purpose_, home_, emp_len_, na.omit(loan_data)

results.claim: Accuracy trap: a model predicting no purchase for 0.1% purchasers is 99.9% accurate and useless.
results.quote:
a model that predicts that each browser will leave without purchasing will be 99.9%
accurate.

results.claim: Lift of 3 in top decile if 0.3% response vs 0.1% random.
results.quote:
If you can get 0.3% response in this top
decile instead of the 0.1% you get overall picking randomly, the algorithm is said
to have a lift (also called gains) of 3 in the top decile.

limits: All examples are in R on one loan dataset; no Python equivalents.
Equations were not preserved in the text extraction (odds ratio factors, formulas).
Chapter is a self-contained excerpt; references to other chapters (KNN, trees, bootstrap) are not included.
Inconsistencies: confusion-matrix prose numbers differ from the printed matrix; the small_business odds ratio is described as reducing odds of default though the coefficient is positive.
SMOTE and cost-based classification are described without numbers or code.
practices: Convert a model's propensity to a decision with a cutoff; lower it when the goal is to find a rare class (Logistic Regression, Predicted Values).
Convert multiclass problems into a series of binary problems, especially when one class dominates (More than two categories).
Use accuracy only as a first step; add precision, recall, specificity, ROC/AUC and lift for rare classes (Evaluating Classification Models).
Treat p-values in logistic regression as relative indicators of variable importance, not formal significance (Assessing the Model).
Undersample the prevalent class when you have tens of thousands of rare-class records; otherwise oversample/bootstrap or weight (Strategies for Imbalanced Data).
Weighting is the easy way to change the loss function for a rare class (Adapting the Loss Function).
Use cost-based expected return, not accuracy or AUC, to pick the cutoff (Cost-Based Classification).
Explore predictions visually; one metric like AUC does not capture model appropriateness (Exploring the Predictions).
Normalise predictors before LDA so discriminant weights serve as variable importance (Discriminant Analysis).
Use naive Bayes when ranking matters since its probabilities are biased (Naive Bayes).

terms.definition: Uses the probability of observing predictor values given an outcome to estimate the probability of outcome Y=i given predictor values; assumes predictors independent given the outcome.
The probability of an outcome after the predictor information has been incorporated.
The function that, when applied to the predictor variables, maximizes the separation of the classes.
The function that maps the probability of belonging to a class with a range from +/- infinity; synonym log odds.
The ratio of success (1) to not success (0).
Characterised by a probability distribution (family) and a link function mapping the response to the predictors.
The percent (or proportion) of cases classified correctly.
The percent of predicted 1s that are actually 1s.
A plot of sensitivity versus specificity as the cutoff changes.
The total area under the ROC curve; 1 is perfect, 0.5 is random.
How effective the model is at identifying comparatively rare 1s at different probability cutoffs.
Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique: creates a synthetic record as a randomly weighted average of a rare-class record and a nearest neighbour.
Improvement in predicted response for an individual case with treatment A versus B, from an A/B test with treatment as predictor.
